docs.title: Gateway Overview
docs.text: The Haddacerra Gateway is a hardware platform engineered to interface Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 (CM4) directly with commercial drone controllers such as the DJI RC-N1 and RC-N3

docs.title: 1. Compute & Interposer Stack
docs.text:
• Carrier Board: Houses the CM4, power delivery network, and an integrated 2000mAh battery for independent operation.
  • Networking: Utilizes a dedicated external Wi-Fi module, explicitly bypassing the CM4's default Broadcom chipset to ensure superior network stability and range and usage of 20 MHz band
  • Daughtercard (Interposer): A Pi-Zero sized PCB that acts as the hardware bridge and interfaces with the controller's control signals. Its ADC channels measure control voltages and hardware status, while its DAC channels provide the outputs used for remote control. The CM4 receives these measurements for monitoring and reporting.

docs.title: 2. Enclosure & Display
docs.text:
• Dimensions: 150mm x 85mm x 24mm.
  • Mounting Integration: The enclosure locks directly into the controller's original retractable phone-mounting arm.
  • Enclosure: Houses the physical switches, power button, battery, and a 2.42" OLED status display.
  • Optional SMA Antenna Expansion: The enclosure includes ports to support external panel antennas.

docs.title: 3. Controller & Smartphone
docs.text:
• Host Compatibility: Fully assembled onto a DJI RC-N1, RC-N2, or RC-N3 chassis.
  • Magnetic Device Mount: Because the Gateway enclosure occupies the factory phone clamp, the operator's smartphone or tablet is relocated to a pre-installed magnetic mount on the controller.
  • Wifi Antenna: Uses a compact, high quality stub antenna positioned horizontally on the back of the DJI RC. Keeping it perpendicular to the main vertical drone antennas helps reduce signal interference and maintains a clean wireless connection without disrupting the drone to RC link.

docs.title: DJI Aircraft and Controller Compatibility
docs.text:
Haddacerra interfaces with the control signals of the DJI RC-N1, RC-N2 and RC-N3 controllers. The original controller retains its normal radio link to the aircraft.

Aircraft compatibility follows the stanard DJI Compatibility chart.

The integrated enclosure is designed to replace the phone mount area on the RC-N1, RC-N2 and RC-N3 controllers, accommodating the gateway as part of the controller assembly.

An additional magnetic smartphone/tablet holder is provided, allowing a smartphone or tablet to be mounted while the controller's mounting arm is occupied by the gateway.

DJI smart controllers with built in screens are not supported by the current enclosure design, which relies on the phone mount area for integration.

docs.title: Crossfire Integration
docs.text: Dedicated Crossfire connection pad allow users to connect a compatible Crossfire control setup directly to the gateway.

docs.title: Enclosure Specifications & Layout
docs.text: The Haddacerra Gateway enclosure is engineered for mechanical durability, component alignment, thermal dissipation, and for a clean fit on the RC N1-3 series RC's.

docs.title: 1. Physical Dimensions & Form Factor
docs.text:
• Dimensions: 150 mm × 85 mm × 24 mm

  • Form Factor: Compact low-profile box designed for portability and ease of use.

docs.title: 2. Material & Fabrication
docs.text:
• Material: PA12S-HP Nylon.

  • Fabrication Method: HP Multi Jet Fusion (MJF)

  • Post-Processing: Surface-dyed finish for wear resistance and aesthetics.

docs.title: Hardware Safety & Fail-Safe Protection Systems
docs.text:
The Haddacerra Gateway is designed to be straightforward and easy to set up, and to work seamlessly with everything from casual consumer setups like the DJI Mini 2 and Mini 3 up to Mavic 3 Pro and other advanced ground control systems. However, we made sure simplicity never comes at the expense of reliability! safety is our absolute top priority. The system integrates hardware-level protection and fail-safe mechanisms directly onto the daughter card and carrier board to safeguard your equipment and the gateway.

The custom carrier board and daughter card architecture integrate protection logics designed to handle electrical stress and crashes while keeping the operator in full control:

docs.title: 1. ESD & Power Protection
docs.text:
• Channel-Wide TVS Diodes: Every signal, control line and switch is equipped with Transient Voltage Suppression (TVS) diodes, clamping ESD and inductive surges safely to ground.

  • USB Power eFuse & Diode: The USB power input rail incorporates a dedicated active eFuse and reverse-blocking diode to protect downstream components from overcurrent faults and voltage backfeeds.

  • RC Snubber Networks: Used to suppress voltage ringing and transient spikes.

docs.title: 2. Watchdog Heartbeat & Automated NC/NO Latching
docs.text:
To prevent a catastrophic loss during NO mode operation: upon a crash, or software lockup, the system features a hardware-monitored fail-safe loop:

  • Continuous Heartbeat Monitoring: The hardware watchdog continuously checks the operational state of the CM4.

  • Automatic NO-to-NC Emergency Latching: If the hardware watchdog detects a CM4 crash or software lockup while operating in NO mode, dedicated hardware logic forces the circuit back to NC (Passthrough Mode), restoring the manual control signal path independently of CM4 software. The fault state triggers an audible alarm. Follow the documented recovery procedure before resuming operation.

  • Alarm: Once the watchdog trips and latches the gateway to NC mode an alarm will sound a long beep notifying the operator the CM4 has crashed, to stop the alarm return the manual toggle to NC mode, land safely and restart the gateway.

docs.title: 3. DAC Baseline Matching & Glitch Prevention
docs.text:
• EEPROM Calibration: Prior to transitioning control states, the system references stored center-voltage profiles from the onboard DACs EEPROM's.

  • Active Calibration: Dead-zones and center values can shift over time specially on potentiometer type joysticks such as on the RC N1-N3, the gateway will automatically read the RC's new values on every boot and make sure they match if not you will be prompted to match them in the UI and lock the new values in the DAC's EEPROMs.

  • Zero-Step Switching: This allows seamless transition between modes, zero firmware interrupts, the gateway is essentially invisible to the RC even during mode switching and startup.

docs.title: 4. OLED Power & Burn-In Protection
docs.text:
• Voltage-Sensing Gate: The 2.42" OLED display remains completely unpowered unless it detects valid active voltage rails from the RC. Even if the gateway is fully booted, the display stays off if the RC is powered off, eliminating idle wear.

  • 180-Second Idle Sleep: Automatically enters a low-power sleep state if sticks remain untouched for 180 seconds, waking upon any stick movement.

docs.title: Technical Specifications
docs.text: The Haddacerra Gateway is an integrated hardware and telemetry bridging system designed for low-latency control interception, dual-mode switching, and Raspberry Pi integration.

docs.title: Hardware & Compute Architecture
docs.text:
Primary Compute Platform: Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 (CM4), mounted on a custom carrier board.

Carrier Board: Integrates the CM4, power-delivery circuitry, internal battery and dedicated Wi-Fi module.

Hardware Interposer: Custom 65 × 30 mm Pi Zero sized daughtercard that connects to the carrier board and handles controller signal interception, switching and monitoring.

Alternative Configuration: A compact assembly using a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W may be considered on request. This is an alternative custom configuration, not the standard Haddacerra Gateway. The CM4-based platform is preferred for the product's reliability requirements.

  • Dedicated Power: Internal rechargeable 2000mAh battrey providing 3-4 hours of operation.

  • Dedicated Wi-Fi Module: Skylabs WG217 Wi-Fi module provides stable and reliable WIFI connection using 20 MHz band on 5GHz.

  • Safety: all lines are ESD protected. Watchdog IC constantly monitors CM4 health. Read more about safety features in safety section.

docs.title: Control Portal UI Reference
docs.text:
The Haddacerra Control Portal (app.haddacerra.com) serves as the client-side interface for managing P2P UDP telemetry, calibration, video monitoring, optional remote phone screen interaction, and monitoring voltage and hardware values.

It is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED TO USE A PC/Laptop as support for external controllers on mobile(Android/iOs) is very tricky and is NOT fully supported.

docs.title: 1. Main Dashboard Layout
docs.text: The portal is organised into three primary panels.

docs.title: Control Centre
docs.text:
• Browser gamepad/controller detection and mapping wizard.
  • Target Gateway/device selection.
  • Control link connect/disconnect and link status.
  • CM4 temperature, control latency, and live roll, pitch, throttle, yaw, and tilt values of the USB controller.

docs.title: Battery & Hardware Diagnostics
docs.text:
• Battery state of charge and voltage.
  • DJI RC Power and NC/NO control-mode indicators.
  • Stick-input ADC voltage readouts.
  • DAC calibration controls and DAC feedback/readback values.

docs.title: Live Video Feed
docs.text:
• WHEP browser playback from MediaMTX.
  • Fullscreen video control.
  • Remote Touch enable/disable and phone acknowledgement state.
  • QR code and Copy RTSP URL action for Haddacerra Screen app.
  • Browser side WHEP video metrics.

docs.title: 2. Connection and Latency Metrics
docs.text:
The dashboard deliberately distinguishes the flight-control path from the video-delivery path.

| Control RTT | Browser ↔ CM4 control/telemetry path | Round-trip timing for the control-side response. It is not the video latency. | | WHEP RTT | Browser ↔ selected MediaMTX WebRTC ICE candidate pair | Network round-trip time for the video peer connection. | | Jitter | Incoming video RTP stream | Variation in video packet arrival timing. | | Packet Loss | Incoming video RTP stream | Rolling estimate of lost video RTP packets. | | Decode FPS | Browser video decoder | Frames decoded per second by the browser. |

Interpreting latency

Neither Control RTT nor WHEP RTT alone measures glass-to-glass camera-to-screen delay. End-to-end video latency is not possible.

docs.title: Stage 1: USB HID Axis Mapping Wizard
docs.text:
• Function: Calibrates and normalizes the connected USB handheld controller inputs across 5 primary channels (AETR + Gimbal Tilt).

  • Operation: Maps stick movements with real-time UI visualizers to verify axis orientation and deadzones.

docs.title: Stage 2: Hardware DAC Voltage Matching
docs.text:
• Function: Calibrates on-board analog outputs to match host transmitter baselines.

  • Operation: Reads center voltages directly from the RC channels, locks in calibration values to onboard DAC EEPROM

docs.title: 3. Telemetry & ADC Monitoring Dashboard
docs.text:
Provides real-time feedback read from the interposer's 12 ADC channels:

  • Passthrough Channels (NC): Monitors voltage levels across manual control lines.

  • Driven Channels (NO): Monitors voltage levels across the DAC output lines.

  • Physical Switch State: Live indication of the state control switch(NC or NO).

  • Power Rail: 12th Channel dedicated to monitor health of the main 5V power rail.

docs.title: 4. Safety & Failsafe Indicators
docs.text:
• Watchdog Status: Confirms active heartbeat pulses from the watchdog IC.

  • Software P2P Health: Monitors P2P UDP tunnel's health

docs.title: 5. QR Code
docs.text: After the control session starts, the portal requests the authenticated stream configuration for the selected device. It displays a QR code containing a tokenised RTSP publishing URL. Scan it with the phone camera to open Haddacerra Screen and import the URL, then tap Start and approve Android screen capture.

docs.title: Extra Features & Utilities
docs.text: This page describes additional capabilities available through the Haddacerra Gateway Control Panel during active operations.

docs.title: Remote State Override
docs.text:
Remote State Override is an administrative control function accessible through the control panel UI that enables software control over the hardware state mode.

Override Safety Warning

Remote State Override is disabled by default. Activating this feature allows software commands to override physical control toggles. Enable this function only when remote hardware state management is explicitly required.

docs.title: Behavior & Logic
docs.text:
• Initial State: Remote State Override must be manually enabled in the gateway configuration settings before use. When left disabled, all software override commands are ignored.

  • Interposer Logic: Executing the override command bypasses the physical toggle switch position, forcing the gateway into NO mode.

  • Fail-Safe Recovery: If power is lost, or CM4 crashes, the hardware automatically disengages the override and reverts to NC mode.

docs.title: Mapped Buttons
docs.text: 2 out of 3 buttons(the camera trigger and the front right button) on the DJI controller are mapped and connected to the interposer. they can be pressed via the UI by pressing the dedicated button, or calibrated to a USB HID buttons to be pressed from the USB controller. the buttons continue to work on the DJI controller as normal.

docs.title: Remote Phone Screen Touch
docs.text:
The Control Portal can send taps and simple swipes to the Android phone running Haddacerra Screen. This lets a remote operator interact with the phone UI while viewing its screen in the portal.

  • Requires Haddacerra Screen and the one-time Android Accessibility permission.
  • Requires local phone-to-CM4 network communication.
  • Uses a dedicated reliable WebRTC DataChannel separate from flight-control messages.
  • Does not use Bluetooth and does not require customers to copy a pairing key.
  • Supports taps and simple swipes; it is not a general-purpose remote keyboard or unrestricted Android automation service.

docs.title: Forget WIFI Network
docs.text: To forget wifi credentials and disconnect from the current active WIFI network, press the dedicated button on the UI, the gateway will be forced into wifi-setup mode where you can re-enter your wifi credentials.

docs.title: Startup Guide
docs.text:
Important: You must power on the Gateway first before turning on the DJI controller. The interposer and CM4 must initialize their bus lines and voltage references prior to the host controller booting up.

Follow these steps to power on, configure network connectivity, and initialize your Haddacerra Gateway system in the field.

docs.title: 1. Power On the Gateway
docs.text: Locate the main toggle switch on the left side of the Gateway enclosure and flip it to the ON position.

docs.title: 2. Connect to WiFi Network
docs.text:
To connect to the CM4 remotely, the gateway requires an active WiFi connection:

  • Automatic Reconnection: Upon boot, the gateway attempts to connect to its last known working WiFi network.

  • Setup Mode Fallback: If it cannot reconnect, it enters WiFi setup mode.

docs.title: Network Setup Procedure
docs.text:
1. Find the open setup network. Its name is similar to Haddacera_setupx201.
  2. Connect your phone or computer to this network to automatically open the portal. The setup portal should open automatically; otherwise find the gateway's address in wifi connection details and enter it into the browser.
  3. Select your local network from the scanned list (or enter the SSID manually), input your WiFi password, and click Submit.
  4. The device saves the credentials and connects to your network, causing the setup network to disappear.
  5. Verify connectivity on the OLED display and the web control panel. If connection fails, the setup network remains active until a successful link is established.

docs.title: 3. Power On the DJI Controller
docs.text: Press and hold the power button on your DJI controller (RC-N1, RC-N2, or RC-N3) as normal. The 2.42" OLED display will illuminate to show the system boot sequence, internal 2000mAh battery voltage, and local network status.

docs.title: 4. Attach Mobile Device
docs.text: Place your smartphone or tablet onto the pre-installed magnetic mount on the controller and connect included USB-C cable.

docs.title: 5. Open the Haddacerra Control Portal
docs.text:
1. Instruct the remote user to log in to the control UI at app.haddacerra.com and establish UDP connection.
  2. Connect any USB gamepad/controller to that computer. A desktop or laptop browser is recommended.
  3. Press any controller button or move an axis so the browser detects the gamepad.
  4. Select the target gateway and choose Establish Control Link.

The video path and the control path are separate. the control path can be active without the video stream being active and vice versa.

docs.title: 6. Start Video with the Haddacerra Screen QR Code (Android Setup)
docs.text:
Haddacerra Screen is our own Android fork of ScreenStream. It retains the RTSP Client publishing path used by the Haddacerra MediaMTX service and adds Haddacerra specific integration, including direct QR import and remote-touch support, and various other improvments and changes nessasary for the system to function.

  1. Download and install the Haddacerra Screen app.
  2. Once the UI has established the session, a QR code will appear on the Live Video Feed left panel, provide this code to the operator of the gateway.
  3. On the Android phone mounted to the DJI controller, open the camera or a QR scanner and scan the QR code.
  4. Select the Haddacerra Screen if Android displays an app chooser.
  5. Haddacerra Screen will import the correct RTSP address, verify the address is entered correctly, and verify stream settings.
  6. Tap Start in Haddacerra Screen.
  7. Accept Android's screen-capture/sharing prompt. Android requires this user confirmation before an app can publish the screen.
  8. The UI will now show your videofeed

docs.title: QR import fallback
docs.text:
If the camera application does not offer Haddacerra Screen for the scanned RTSP link:

  1. Use Copy RTSP URL in the portal.
  2. Open Haddacerra Screen.
  3. Select RTSP Client and paste the complete URL into Server Address.
  4. Tap Start and approve Android screen capture.

docs.title: 6A. Moblin Apple iOS app setup (Apple setup)
docs.text:
1. Download and install the Moblin application from the App tore.

  2. Open the control centre by swiping down from the top right corner, press the plus icon, and click 'Add a Control', click on the screen recording icon. this will add screen recording to your controls.

  3. Open the Moblin app, press on settings on the top right, click on 'Scenes' and remove the existing scenes, create a new scene, press on 3 lines icon on the left of your new scene and change video source to 'Screen Capture', press back button and return to settings.

  4. Inside the Moblin app settings click on 'Streams' and remove existing streams. Create a new stream, and in the stream wizard press Custom, Select RTMP(S),

docs.title: 7. Enable Remote Phone Touch (Android only)
docs.text:
Remote Touch allows the browser operator to tap or swipe the phone screen through the live video stream. It is useful for dismissing on-screen prompts, opening DJI Fly settings, or interacting with a phone UI without asking the field operator to reach for the phone.

Remote Touch is a sensitive operation on Android and requires several special permissions to be given in order to work, this is done for obvious safety reasons.

  1. Make sure the Phone and CM4 Gateway are on the same WiFi network.
  2. Go to Settings -> Remote touchscreen to see the status of the remote touchscreen service. follow these steps to install for the first time.
  3. In your Android device open Setting and tap Apps, find Haddacerra Screen app, Tap on the 3 dots on the top right corner of the screen, click Allow restrected setting.
  4. Either click on the shortcut in the Haddacerra screen settings or go directly to Settings -> Features -> Accessibility . click the Haddacerra Screen app, and enable "Use Haddacerra Screen".
  5. Verify in Haddacerra Screen -> Settings -> Remote touchscreen that Accessibility service is enabled.
  6. In the Live Video Feed panel, select REMOTE TOUCH · ON once the control channel and phone connection are available.
  7. Click or tap the displayed video to send a tap to the corresponding point on the phone. Drag across the video to send a swipe.

Note: Step 4 will have to be repeated after the app is completely reset. Step 3 is only performed once after installation.

Remote touch currently supports single taps and swipes only. It is not a remote keyboard.

docs.title: Control Modes (NC & NO)
docs.text:
The Gateway uses hardware switches to control whether stick inputs are routed locally or driven by the onboard CM4 compute core.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Control Layout                    │
├─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│     NC Mode    │ Controller Sticks ──► Drone (Normal)  │
│                │ CM4 Core          ──► Monitoring Only │
├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│     NO Mode    │ Remote / Edge AI  ──► CM4 ──► Drone   │
│                │ Controller Sticks ──► Overridden      │
└─────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 1. NC Mode (Manual Passthrough)
docs.text:
By default, the system operates in NC Mode:

  • The physical controller sticks are wired normally.

  • The operator retains full manual flight authority as normal.

  • The Gateway acts strictly as a telemetry display.

docs.title: 2. NO Mode (CM4 / Remote Control)
docs.text:
To hand off control to an automated script, AI loop, or remote operator:

  1. Instruct the remote user to log in to the control UI at app.haddacerra.com and establish UDP connection.

  2. Locate the state control switch on the left side of the Gateway enclosure

  3. Toggle the state switch to NO Mode.

  4. The interposer will engage the CM4 control lines, allowing the CM4 to send flight commands.

docs.title: Reverting to Manual Control
docs.text:
To instantly restore manual pilot control at any time:

  • Flip the state switch back to NC Mode.

  • RC regains full manual control.

docs.title: Battery and Charging
docs.text:
An internal 2000mah battery is included and will run the gateway for around 3-4 hours of usage on its own.

To charge, connect a USB-C cable from any charger to the port on the right side of the enclosure.

It is possible to use gateway during charging, this way the battery is only being charged and the gateway can run from a wall charger or a larger external battery.

Charging takes about 30-40 minutes.

Make sure to always monitor the battery health on the main status display.

docs.title: NAT Traversal & Network Bridge
docs.text:
The Haddacerra network bridge is designed to provide a low latency, encrypted, and reliable link between the ground control web interface and the CM4 hardware gateway.

Remote deployments may use cellular networks, network address translation (NAT), or carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT). Because direct connectivity cannot be assumed in these environments, the bridge combines WebSocket signaling, Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE), STUN/TURN traversal, and encrypted WebRTC DataChannel transport for seamless connectivity.

The system prioritises direct connectivity whenever a viable path can be established, with TURN available as a relay fallback when direct connectivity is unavailable or unsuitable.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The network bridge relies on three primary components working together during session establishment and operation.

The Ground Client (Browser): Initiates the flight session, renders telemetry dashboards, processes physical USB controller inputs, and presents the video stream.

The CM4 Agent: Runs locally on the hardware gateway, processes incoming control payloads, drives the hardware DAC outputs, collects ADC measurements, and manages local monitoring and peripheral state.

The Coordination & Relay Infrastructure: A cloud hosted signaling server handles WebSocket rendezvous and session negotiation, while a dedicated Coturn server provides STUN services and TURN relay connectivity.

Signaling is used to establish the connection. Normal control and telemetry traffic is carried over the established WebRTC DataChannel rather than through the signaling server.

docs.title: 1. Signaling and Session Handshake
docs.text:
Before direct or relayed data can flow between the ground client and the CM4 agent, the endpoints must exchange connection information and establish the WebRTC session.

WebSocket rendezvous: When the user initiates a link, the browser and CM4 agent establish persistent WebSocket connections to the centralized signaling service.

SDP Offer/Answer Exchange: The browser generates a Session Description Protocol (SDP) offer describing the session and DataChannel capabilities. The offer is forwarded to the CM4 agent through the signaling service. The CM4 agent generates the corresponding SDP answer and returns it through signaling.

Trickle ICE: ICE candidates are exchanged as they become available, allowing connectivity checks and session establishment to proceed without waiting for all candidates to be gathered first.

The signaling service coordinates session establishment; it does not carry the normal control and telemetry DataChannel traffic.

docs.title: 2. Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) & NAT Traversal
docs.text:
Once session negotiation begins, the browser and CM4 agent gather network candidates and use ICE connectivity checks to determine which communication paths are viable.

ICE can use several candidate types:

Host Candidates: Local network addresses available on the endpoint. These may provide a direct path when the endpoints can communicate over the same network or another reachable network route.

Server-Reflexive Candidates (STUN): Addresses and port mappings observed by a STUN server. These can help establish direct connectivity through NAT when the resulting mappings are reachable by the other endpoint.

Relay Candidates (TURN): Addresses allocated through a TURN server. These provide a relayed path when direct connectivity cannot be established or when the connection policy requires a relay.

ICE evaluates viable candidate pairs and selects a working path according to candidate priorities, connectivity checks, and the configured connection policy. These candidate types are not three mandatory sequential stages. A TURN candidate may be gathered while direct connectivity is also being tested; gathering a relay candidate does not mean that the relay is carrying traffic.

docs.title: Direct Connectivity and TURN Fallback
docs.text:
Haddacerra prioritises direct connectivity whenever a suitable direct path can be established. This avoids unnecessary relay hops and helps minimise control latency.

Being behind CGNAT does not automatically require a TURN relay. Depending on the carrier's NAT behaviour, port mappings, and firewall restrictions, ICE may still establish a direct peer-to-peer path.

When a suitable direct path is unavailable or unsuitable, ICE can select a TURN relay candidate. In this case, control and telemetry packets are forwarded through the configured Coturn server. When ICE selects a direct candidate pair, the DataChannel traffic bypasses the TURN relay.

This approach combines low-latency direct connectivity where possible with relay support for more restrictive network environments.

TURN improves connectivity options but cannot guarantee connectivity under every possible network condition. Successful relay operation depends on server availability, network reachability, valid credentials, and compatible network policies.

docs.title: 3. Secure Coturn Relay Integration
docs.text:
To prevent unauthorized relay usage and abuse of cloud resources, the Coturn relay uses time-limited credentials generated through the configured shared-secret authentication mechanism.

Rather than embedding a permanent TURN password in the client, the system provisions temporary credentials for session establishment. HMAC-SHA1 is used by the configured credential mechanism to derive the authentication password from the shared secret and credential username. Coturn validates the supplied credentials when the client requests a relay allocation.

These credentials authenticate access to the relay service; they do not themselves encrypt the control payload. DataChannel encryption is provided separately by DTLS.

When TURN is selected, Coturn forwards the encrypted traffic between the WebRTC peers. It does not need to decrypt the application data to relay the packets.

docs.title: 4. Encrypted Transport & DataChannel Stack
docs.text:
After session establishment, operational control commands, feedback, and telemetry are carried over a dedicated WebRTC DataChannel using SCTP over DTLS over UDP.

Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS): DTLS provides encryption and integrity protection for DataChannel traffic between the browser and CM4 agent. When a TURN relay is used, the DataChannel remains encrypted between the peers while Coturn forwards the packets.

Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP): SCTP operates over DTLS and provides DataChannel message transport. The control channel is configured for unordered delivery with retransmissions disabled, favouring timely control updates over guaranteed delivery of every individual message.

This configuration avoids waiting for ordered delivery or retransmission of lost control messages. However, messages may still be delayed or lost, and the configuration does not eliminate network congestion or guarantee a fixed end-to-end latency. Actual responsiveness depends on network conditions.

docs.title: OLED Display & Power-State Reference
docs.text: The Haddacerra Gateway features an integrated OLED display designed for real-time telemetry readout, system state verification.

docs.title: 1. Power-State Gating & Safety
docs.text:
To prevent screen burn-in and eliminate unnecessary power draw, the OLED display operates under strict conditions:

  • RC-Dependent Activation: The OLED display remains completely powered off unless it detects valid voltage inputs from the RC. If the radio is powered down, the display stays off even when the gateway is active.

  • Instant Wake Trigger: Pressing the RC's power button or turning it on immediately supplies valid voltage levels to the interposer lines, triggering the display to wake up instantly.

docs.title: 2. Idle Timeout & Sleep
docs.text:
The display uses activity monitoring to protect against burn-in during prolonged stationary use:

  • Active Tracking: During standard operation, stick movement keeps the display active.

  • 180-Second Idle Timeout: If the operator leaves the sticks untouched (such as when operating in remote NO mode), the display automatically enters sleep mode after 180 seconds of inactivity. Any subsequent stick movement instantly wakes the panel.

docs.title: 3. Operational Display Modes
docs.text: The OLED interface switches its readout automatically depending on the active control state:

docs.title: NC Mode (Passthrough)
docs.text:
When operating on direct manual control, the screen displays:

  • Battery Health: Real-time power supply status.

  • Link Latency: Round-trip telemetry delay.

  • UDP Connection State: Active/inactive status of the P2P network tunnel.

  • Internet Latency: Network ping performance.

docs.title: NO Mode (Remote / CM4 Control)
docs.text:
When operating via the CM4 or remote internet control, the screen switches to telemetry visualization:

  • DAC Axis Visualizers: Two graphical coordinate boxes with center dots representing live DAC output values (reflecting USB controller stick inputs), allowing direct visual verification of remote or script-driven stick movements.

  • System Status: Battery health and connection integrity readouts.

docs.title: Remote Phone Screen Control
docs.text:
Remote Touch allows an authorised browser user to interact with the Android phone that is streaming the live screen to the Haddacerra UI. It is designed for simple operational actions such as dismissing alerts, changing settings, zooming in on a map, etc. without asking the field operator to reach for the phone.

Remote Touch is an optional feature. It does not replace the flight control path and does not provide unrestricted control of the Android phone.

docs.title: 1. Components and Data Flow
docs.text:
Browser operator
  |  click / drag on the video image
  v
Reliable WebRTC DataChannel: "screen-input"
  |  DTLS-protected peer connection
  v
CM4 Gateway agent
  |  local authenticated TCP session
  v
Haddacerra Screen on Android
  |  Android AccessibilityService dispatchGesture()
  v
Android screen: tap / swipe

The screen input channel is separate from the existing flight control channel. The control channel remains configured for low latency control updates; discrete screen gestures use a separate reliable, ordered DataChannel so taps and swipes are not silently discarded or reordered by the control channel's delivery policy.

Remote Touch currently supports single taps and simple swipes. It does not inject arbitrary key presses, type text, execute shell commands, or browse the Android accessibility tree.

docs.title: 2. Requirements
docs.text:
• Haddacerra Screen must be installed on the Android phone that publishes the screen.
  • Android's Haddacerra Screen Remote Input Accessibility service must be enabled by the user.
  • Haddacerra Screen must be running and listening on the local network.
  • The CM4 and phone must be able to communicate on the same local Wi-Fi/hotspot network.
  • The browser portal's control session and screen-input DataChannel must be active.

Some Wi-Fi hotspots, guest networks, and enterprise access points isolate wireless clients. If client isolation is enabled, the phone and CM4 may have internet access but still be unable to discover or connect to each other locally.

docs.title: 3. Network and Security Notes
docs.text:
• The browser-to-CM4 WebRTC DataChannel uses the WebRTC DTLS transport.
  • The normal flight-control channel is separate; disabling Remote Touch does not disable the flight-control channel.
  • The Android user remains responsible for granting and revoking the Accessibility permission.

docs.title: Video Streaming Setup Guide
docs.text:
The Haddacerra Gateway hardware focuses on low-latency stick interception, telemetry routing, and hardware safety overrides only.

Android captures the phone display and publishes it to MediaMTX over RTSP; the browser receives the stream through WHEP/WebRTC.

docs.title: 1. Architecture & Default Server Provisioning
docs.text:
Android phone / tablet
  DJI Fly + Haddacerra Screen
             |
             | RTSP publish (authenticated URL)
             v
      MediaMTX server
       /           \
      /             \
 WHEP/WebRTC       RTSP clients
      |
      v
Browser portal video panel

When you initiate a UDP connection through the Web Control Portal (app.haddacerra.com), the system manages RTSP streaming endpoints for low-latency monitoring.

  • Default Managed Server: By default, you can utilize the built-in MediaMTX server provided with the Haddacerra ecosystem. When your UDP connection starts, a QR code containing your unique RTSP link will appear automatically.

  • Self-Hosted Alternative: You are not locked into the default server. If you prefer to run your own server, you can host your own MediaMTX, ignore the provided QR code/link, and point your browser directly to your custom RTSP endpoint.

docs.title: 2. Haddacerra Screen Android App
docs.text:
Haddacerra Screen is the Haddacerra-maintained fork of ScreenStream, based on upstream 4.5.0. The Haddacerra build uses the ad-free ScreenStream implementation as its base and retains the existing RTSP Client pipeline. It adds Haddacerra-specific QR link import and the optional remote-touch receiver.

The Haddacerra Screen RTSP fork was updated to keep the existing RTP SSRC and packetizer sequence across this encoder reconfiguration, update codec parameter sets in-band, and request a fresh keyframe. This avoids changing the RTP SSRC in the middle of an existing RTSP publishing session, which strict receivers such as MediaMTX can reject.

The app is intended to run alongside the normal drone application. It captures and publishes the Android display after the user approves Android's screen-capture prompt; the operator can continue using compatible apps such as DJI Fly normally.

docs.title: 3. Viewing the Stream
docs.text:
Once the stream is live, you can monitor the video feed using either of the following methods:

  • In-Portal Integration: If using the default server or you entered your custom server URL to the UI, your stream will show on the right side of the UI.

  • Dedicated Browser Tab (Recommended): For a cleaner and larger view open a separate browser tab pointing directly to the stream URL.

The Live Video Feed panel reports browser-side WebRTC statistics such as:

| WHEP RTT | Round-trip time for the selected browser-to-MediaMTX ICE candidate pair. |

| Jitter | Variation in incoming video RTP packet arrival timing as reported by the browser. |

| Packet loss | Rolling video RTP packet-loss estimate over the latest statistics interval. |

| Decode FPS | Video frames decoded per second by the browser. |
